1.taunt: Do you count as the scrolls count, little ember?

scrolls.title: Counting from Zero
scrolls.insight: A list's first item lives at index 0, so the third item is row[2].

scrolls.title: Counting Backwards
scrolls.insight: Negative indexes count from the end: row[-1] is always the last item.

scrolls.title: The Slice Spell
scrolls.insight: A slice [a:b] starts at a and stops just before b. Strings slice too.

scrolls.title: Lists Can Change
scrolls.insight: append() adds to the end. Assigning to an index replaces that item.

questions.explanation: Indexes start at 0, so xs[1] is the second item.
questions.hint: Children count from one. Scrolls do not.

questions.explanation: xs[0] is 5 and xs[2] is 7, the first and the last.
questions.hint: Three items. Which number names the last of them?

questions.explanation: i + 1 is 2, and index 2 is the third item, 9.
questions.hint: Do the sum first. Then count the way the hollow taught you.

questions.explanation: -1 counts back from the end, so it is always the last item.
questions.hint: A minus sign does not mean nothing. It means turn around.

questions.explanation: len counts all five items. xs[-2] is second from the end: 1.
questions.hint: len() counts like a merchant. -2 walks in from the far end.

questions.explanation: xs[-1] is the last item, 4. xs[0] is the first, 1.
questions.hint: One end times the other end. Which ends?

questions.explanation: The slice starts at index 1 and stops before index 4.
questions.hint: A slice never takes the item at its last number.

questions.explanation: [:3] starts at the beginning and stops before index 3.
questions.hint: Letters line up just like list items do.

questions.explanation: append() adds one item to the end, so there are now four.
questions.hint: The list grew. len() only ever gives back a number.

questions.explanation: Assigning to xs[1] replaces the second item. Nothing is inserted.
questions.hint: Replacing is not inserting. And which one is [1]?

2.taunt: Every key knows its bucket. Do you?

scrolls.title: Keys and Values
scrolls.insight: A dict maps each key to a value. You look things up by key, not by position.

scrolls.title: The Hashing Rune
scrolls.insight: A dict hashes the key to pick a bucket, then looks only there. No searching.

scrolls.title: One Key, One Value
scrolls.insight: The same key always hashes to the same bucket, so writing it again replaces the value.

scrolls.title: Keys Must Not Change
scrolls.insight: A list can change, so its hash could not be trusted. Keys must be str, int, tuple...

scrolls.title: Asking Politely
scrolls.insight: bag["clay"] would raise KeyError. get() hands back a default instead.

questions.explanation: Looking up a key gives back its value, not the key.
questions.hint: The key opens the box. What is inside the box?

questions.explanation: Assigning to a new key adds it. len counts the keys.
questions.hint: A new key is not an error. It is a new resident.

questions.explanation: values() gives 3 and 5, and sum adds them.
questions.hint: Count what is inside, not how many boxes.

questions.explanation: The same key always hashes the same way, so it lands in the same bucket.
questions.hint: If the rune changed its mind, how would any vault find anything?

questions.explanation: x already exists, so its value is replaced in place.
questions.hint: One key. One bucket. Room for one value.

questions.explanation: Both entries share one key. The later one wins.
questions.hint: Two travellers, one bed. Who sleeps there last?

questions.explanation: clay is missing, so get() returns the default you gave it.
questions.hint: Ask politely and you are never refused. You get what you asked.

questions.explanation: in checks the keys. Only ash is there.
questions.hint: in only asks yes or no.

questions.explanation: A list can change, so it has no hash and cannot be a key.
questions.hint: What may change cannot be trusted with a bucket.

3.taunt: Round and round the kiln turns. Where does it stop?

scrolls.title: The Loop Rune
scrolls.insight: range(3) counts 0, 1, 2. It stops before the number you give it.

scrolls.title: Start, Stop, Step
scrolls.insight: range(start, stop, step) begins at start, adds step, and stops before stop.

scrolls.title: Gathering Embers
scrolls.insight: Start the total before the loop, then add to it on every pass.

scrolls.title: Loops That Wait
scrolls.insight: while repeats until its condition is False. It checks before every pass.

questions.explanation: range(4) starts at 0 and stops before 4.
questions.hint: The kiln starts cold, at nothing. And it never reaches the end.

questions.explanation: 5, 8 and 9 are greater than 4. Each adds one to count.
questions.hint: The loop visits every one. Only some pass the gate.

questions.explanation: Start at 2 and step by 2. 8 would pass the stop of 7.
questions.hint: Walk it out loud: start, add the step, check the stop.

questions.explanation: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Stop minus start is 5.
questions.hint: Ten is never reached. Count what is.

questions.explanation: A negative step counts down. It stops before reaching 0.
questions.hint: Steps may walk backwards. The stop still bars the door.

questions.explanation: 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 is 6. range(4) never gives 4.
questions.hint: List the numbers range hands out before you add a single one.

questions.explanation: Each letter is put in front of the others, so the word comes out reversed.
questions.hint: Watch which side each new letter joins.

questions.explanation: 10 becomes 6, then 2. Now 2 > 3 is False, so the loop stops.
questions.hint: Check the condition before each pass, not after.

questions.explanation: The loop stops as soon as i < 3 is False, which first happens at 3.
questions.hint: The while asks one question. When is the answer first no?

4.taunt: True or False, little ember? My gates already know.

scrolls.title: Yes or No
scrolls.insight: A comparison gives back True or False. == asks equal?, != asks not equal?

scrolls.title: and, or, not
scrolls.insight: and needs both sides True. or needs just one. not flips True and False.

scrolls.title: The Fork
scrolls.insight: Python tries each branch from the top and runs only the first one that is True.

scrolls.title: Empty Means False
scrolls.insight: 0, empty strings and empty lists count as False. Nearly everything else is True.

scrolls.title: Chains & Remainders
scrolls.insight: 1 < x < 9 checks both sides at once. x % 2 == 1 is True for odd x. not goes last.

questions.explanation: >= allows equal. > does not.
questions.hint: Is seven more than itself? Is it at least itself?

questions.explanation: x * 2 is 8, so the comparison is True. == gives a bool, not a number.
questions.hint: == asks a question. What kind of thing answers it?

questions.explanation: not False is True, and True and True is True.
questions.hint: Flip the second one first, then join them.

questions.explanation: a > 5 is False, but a < 4 is True, and or needs only one.
questions.hint: or is generous. One True is enough.

questions.explanation: 2 > 1 is True but 3 > 4 is False, and and needs both.
questions.hint: and is strict. Check both sides.

questions.explanation: n > 10 is False, n > 5 is True, so the elif runs and the rest is skipped.
questions.hint: Walk down the fork. Stop at the first True.

questions.explanation: t > 1 is True, so the elif is never checked, even though it is True too.
questions.hint: Two branches are True. How many run?

questions.explanation: An empty list counts as False, so the else branch runs.
questions.hint: Is there anything in the bag?

questions.explanation: "0" is a string with one character in it. Only the empty string is False.
questions.hint: Look at the quotes. Is that a number?

questions.explanation: 2 < x is True but x < 5 is False. A chain needs every link.
questions.hint: Read it as two checks joined by and.

questions.explanation: n % 2 == 1 is True for 1, 3 and 5: three odd numbers.
questions.hint: Odd numbers leave a remainder of one.

5.taunt: A spell that returns nothing builds nothing, little ember.

scrolls.title: Naming a Spell
scrolls.insight: def names a block of code. Calling double(4) runs it with n set to 4.

scrolls.title: Handing Back
scrolls.insight: return hands a value back to the caller, to store in a name or use at once.

scrolls.title: Nothing Returned
scrolls.insight: print shows a value but hands nothing back. With no return, a call gives None.

scrolls.title: Default Arguments
scrolls.insight: by=2 is a default: used when the call leaves it out, replaced when it doesn't.

scrolls.title: Inside Stays Inside
scrolls.insight: A name set inside a function is its own. The x outside is left alone.

questions.explanation: Calling triple(5) runs the body with n = 5 and returns 5 * 3.
questions.hint: Put the number in for n, then do the sum.

questions.explanation: add(2, 3) returns 5 first, then 5 * 2 is 10.
questions.hint: The call finishes before the multiplying starts.

questions.explanation: The inner call returns 2, then area(3, 2) is 6.
questions.hint: Start with the innermost call.

questions.explanation: return ends the function at once, so the print after it never runs.
questions.hint: Does anything happen after return?

questions.explanation: -3 takes the early return. 4 skips the if and reaches the last line.
questions.hint: Each call takes its own path.

questions.explanation: The sum is worked out and thrown away. Without return, the call gives None.
questions.hint: Something was made. Was it handed back?

questions.explanation: A bare return hands back None, so the check is True.
questions.hint: return with nothing after it returns... what?

questions.explanation: lay() uses the default 3. lay(5) replaces it with 5.
questions.hint: When nothing is passed, the default steps in.

questions.explanation: The call passes "?", so the default "!" is not used.
questions.hint: A default is only a fallback.

questions.explanation: grow sets its own n. The n outside is untouched.
questions.hint: What happens inside the spell stays inside it.

questions.explanation: A function can read a name from outside. It just can't reassign it.
questions.hint: Reading is allowed. Only setting makes a new name.

6.taunt: Can you read a whole forge in one line, little ember?

scrolls.title: Lists in One Line
code: squares = [n * n for n in range(4)]
scrolls.insight: [expr for n in seq] builds a list: one expr for every n, in order.

scrolls.title: The Sieve
code: odds = [n for n in range(8) if n % 2 == 1]
scrolls.insight: An if at the end keeps only the items it says True for.

scrolls.title: Words In, Words Out
scrolls.insight: Any expression works on the left: a method call, len(), an index, a sum.

scrolls.title: Dicts Too
scrolls.insight: Curly braces and key: value build a dict instead of a list.

scrolls.title: Still a List
scrolls.insight: A comprehension is still a list, so sum, len and max all work on it.

questions.explanation: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2, and each gets 1 added.
questions.hint: List what range gives first. Then change each.

questions.explanation: Each item is multiplied by 10, and the results form a new list.
questions.hint: One item in, one item out.

code: xs = [n * n for n in range(5)]
questions.explanation: range(5) stops at 4, and the last square is 4 * 4.
questions.hint: Where does range(5) stop?

code: print([n for n in range(10) if n > 6])
questions.explanation: Only items where n > 6 is True are kept: 7, 8 and 9.
questions.hint: The if is a sieve. What falls through?

code: print(len([c for c in w if c == "a"]))
questions.explanation: Three of the letters are a, so the kept list has three items.
questions.hint: Count only the letters that pass the if.

code: print([x for x in xs if x > 2])
questions.explanation: Only 1 fails x > 2. The rest are kept in their order.
questions.hint: Which ones are bigger than two?

code: print([x * 2 for x in xs if x % 2])
questions.explanation: x % 2 is 1, which counts as True, for odd x. So 1, 3, 5 are kept, then doubled.
questions.hint: The filter runs before the doubling.

questions.explanation: w[0] is each word's first letter.
questions.hint: Index zero. You learned this in the Hollow.

questions.explanation: len is called on each word, giving a list of three lengths.
questions.hint: One length per word.

code: d = {n: n * n for n in range(3)}
questions.explanation: Each n becomes a key, and n * n its value.
questions.hint: Curly braces. key: value.

questions.explanation: The key "ab" maps to len("ab"), which is 2.
questions.hint: Look up the key, get its value.

questions.explanation: The list is [0, 1, 2, 3], and its sum is 6.
questions.hint: Build the list, then add it up.

questions.explanation: The list is [0, 1, 2, 0, 1]: its largest is 2, and it holds five items.
questions.hint: Write out the list before you measure it.
